messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Frank was seventy-six, a cashier for the past thirty years at a Midtown grocery store, and he could not remember the last time he had driven himself anywhere. The refusal had grown quietly, like frost spreading across a window, starting the morning after the attack. He had been working his register when the first mortar round hit the parking lot. The blast threw him against the wall; the ceiling tiles fell like heavy snow. In the chaos that followed—the screaming, the blood on the linoleum, the woman who had been third in line now silent on the floor—Frank had grabbed his manager’s keys and driven two miles with his hands shaking so badly he could barely steer. That drive, that desperate escape, was now the thing he could not repeat. He would not get behind a wheel, and he would not sit in a passenger seat either. When his daughter offered to pick him up for Sunday dinner, he said the store needed him. He had not seen her in four months.

At work, he stood behind his register and watched the customers. He watched their hands, their eyes, the way they moved through the aisles. He was certain that any one of them could be carrying something, that danger could walk through the automatic doors at any second. The world, he had come to believe, was a dangerous place—not vaguely, but specifically, intimately. The attack had proven that. He kept his gaze moving, scanning exits, scanning faces. At night, when he finally lay down in his small apartment, his body refused to relax. He would lie in bed, fully dressed, listening to the street noises, unable to drift off because staying alert felt like the only thing keeping him alive. Sleep was a surrender he could no longer afford.

When memories of the explosion came—and they came often, mostly as sharp, silent pictures—he felt nothing. He could see the ceiling tiles falling, see the woman’s shopping bag spill its contents, but it was as if he were watching a stranger. That numbness frightened him more than the terror ever had. Sometimes the memory was so vivid it felt like the attack was happening again, right there in the cereal aisle at work, and he would grip the register counter until his knuckles whitened. “I’m here,” he would whisper to himself, but the words felt hollow.

He had started to think about why the event had happened to him. He was not a soldier. He was a cashier. He had not asked for any of it. The question circled endlessly: why him, why that day, why that store. He found no answer, only a growing certainty that he was no longer capable of the things that had once defined him—being a dependable father, a steady worker, a man who could laugh at his grandchildren’s jokes. He had stopped laughing. He pushed away good feelings because they felt dangerous, as if joy invited disaster. He had lost his faith in people, in life, in the God he had never prayed to much but had assumed existed. None of it felt real anymore.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a heart attack scare—chest pain that turned out to be panic—and a note from his manager saying he had been missing too many shifts. Frank sat in the waiting room, watching the door. He was afraid of what he would find if he looked inside himself, but he was also tired of being watchful. He wanted to sleep. He wanted to drive to his daughter’s house. He did not know if therapy could give him those things, but he had run out of other places to go.
